section_summary: This section covers diplomatic reporting from 1930 to 1932 on communist, radical, and subversive activities in Japan and East Asia. It details the prosecution of Japanese Communist Party leaders under the Peace Preservation Act, student radicalism, labor unrest, and the formation of underground networks linked to the Comintern. Additionally, reports from Harbin and Riga analyze Soviet apparatuses training Asian cadres, alongside Moscow's propaganda strategies against Japanese imperialism and military mobilization in Manchuria.

subfiles.about: Response to State Department instruction regarding coverage of Russo-Japanese relations in the Japanese press.
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle, Jr., American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The Embassy acknowledges receipt of instruction No. 671 regarding previous discussions on Russo-Japanese relations. It reports that after an examination of the vernacular press, no references to the committee discussions were found.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 27: Russo-Japanese Relations in the Japanese Press

subfiles.about: Report on the indictment and preliminary court findings against thirty-five leaders of the Japanese Communist Party.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Counselor of Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Reports that thirty-five alleged Japanese communists arrested during police raids in 1928 and 1929 were found guilty in preliminary court and committed for public trial. Gaku Sano is identified as the first leader facing trial under the death penalty provisions of the amended Peace Preservation Act of 1928. The despatch provides an extensive historical account of the Japanese Communist Party's underground founding, Comintern funding and guidance, internal doctrinal disputes, and student and labor recruitment.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 122: Indictment and Trial of Japanese Communists

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and extract regarding the arrest of 44 individuals in Karafuto for communist activities.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference file note and monthly report extract regarding the arrest of 44 persons, including seven women and several employees of the Karafuto Government, for alleged communist activities. The investigation stemmed from the publication of a radical magazine.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00B/38: Arrest of Communists in Karafuto

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and extract reporting preliminary trial results for communists arrested in Karafuto.
subfiles.summary: Transmits an extract reporting that thirteen of the forty-four individuals arrested in Karafuto were found guilty in preliminary proceedings under the Peace Preservation Law. The group had organized a local communist party committee and attempted to incite strikes in local mills and factories.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00B/39 (P.R./33): Trial of Karafuto Communists

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and extract reporting on a violent May Day communist riot in Kawasaki.
subfiles.summary: Details the lifting of police censorship regarding a May Day clash at Inari Shrine in Kawasaki, where eighteen members of the Young Communists' Alliance armed with swords, spears, and revolvers clashed with police. Sixteen persons were arrested, with three leaders including Sakuzo Abe charged with attempted manslaughter and weapons offenses.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00B/39 (P.R./36): Communist Riots at Kawasaki

subfiles.about: Consular despatch transmitting an intelligence report on Soviet training schools and communist networks in the Far East.
subfiles.from: E. B. Thomas, American Consul, Harbin
subfiles.summary: Transmits an intelligence memorandum prepared by a White Russian working with Harbin staff headquarters describing Soviet institutions that train foreign communist cadres, notably the Sun Yat-sen Institute and GPU courses in Moscow and eastern Siberia. The report details theoretical indoctrination, espionage instruction, military sabotage training, and infiltration into armed forces and labor groups across China, Korea, Japan, and the Pacific islands. Consul Thomas notes that while the institutional apparatus exists, several specific claims and student figures are likely exaggerated.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5150: The Organization of Communistic Propaganda in Korea, China, Japan and the Islands

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet concerning Soviet diplomatic representations over an assassination attempt on a trade official in Japan.
subfiles.summary: File note on a Soviet communique protesting an assassination attempt on the Soviet commercial chief and anti-Soviet Japanese fishing interests.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00B/41: Attempted Assassination of Soviet Commercial Chief

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and extract reporting the arrest of Yoshio Iwata and the disruption of party reorganization efforts.
subfiles.summary: Reports that police frustrated a fourth attempt to reorganize the banned Japan Communist Party by arresting ringleader Yoshio Iwata and his associates. The arrests followed student handbill distributions during national celebrations commemorating Emperor Jimmu Tenno.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00B/42: Frustration of Communist Reorganization

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and extract regarding the exposure of a radical plot to burn the Imperial Diet building.
subfiles.summary: Covers police disclosures of a foiled communist plot to burn down the Diet building during its legislative session. Out of 173 indicted suspects, 92 were individuals with higher education, including organizers linked to Tokyo Imperial University led by Seigen Tanaka.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00B/43: Communist Plot to Burn Diet Building

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and extract reporting disruptions during the second public trial of Japanese communists.
subfiles.summary: Describes the second public trial of forty Japanese communists commencing on July 7, marked by frequent interruptions, political speeches from defendants, and demonstrations outside the courthouse. Proceedings grew contentious after the judge attempted to restrict public access to prevent radical songs and perceived insults to the Imperial Family.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00B/44: Trial of the Japanese Communists

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet summarizing an evaluation of political radicalism and reaction in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Notes despatch No. 561 from Tokyo identifying communism and fascism as the two most dangerous underlying socio-political currents in Japan.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00B/45: Undercurrents of Communism and Fascism

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum analyzing Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 615 on social unrest and radicalism.
subfiles.summary: Reviews Laurence Salisbury's study on Japanese radicalism, noting that communism represents virtually the entire organized radical movement in Japan. It highlights that severe police pressure and the nationalist wave linked to Manchurian expansion have eclipsed communist strength, though student participation remains an area of major official concern.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Radicalism in Japan

subfiles.about: Comprehensive survey of communist and radical movements, history, doctrine, student groups, and organization in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Presents an exhaustive analysis drafted by Laurence Salisbury examining the history, factions, and current condition of radicalism in Japan. It surveys early socialism, the founding and successive suppressions of the Japan Communist Party, student organizations like the Shin-jin-kai, and the impact of the Peace Preservation Law. The report concludes that while military reactionism has temporarily suppressed overt communist influence, economic hardship and student sympathizers sustain underground networks; an English translation of the 13-point 1926 party platform is appended.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 615: Radicalism in Japan

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum summarizing Riga despatch No. 510 on Japanese Young Communist tactics in the military.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum on a Riga report of a Japanese Young Communist article instructing cadres to accept mobilization to obtain arms and subvert the army from within.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Subversive Activities of Japanese Young Communists

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting a translated manifesto detailing Japanese Young Communist tactics within the imperial armed forces.
subfiles.summary: Transmits a translation of a programmatic manifesto titled 'We are for the Defeat of "Our" Bourgeoisie' published in Moscow's Internatsional Molodezhi from the clandestine Japanese organ Leninskaya Molodezh. The document instructs young communists not to evade conscription, but rather to enter the ranks, establish factory-to-barracks contact committees, demand improved soldier conditions, organize mutinies, and surrender to or unite with the Red Army in wartime. Cole analyzes the piece as a prime example of Comintern military directives for foreign affiliates during imperialist wars.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 510: Subversive Activities of the Japanese Young Communists

subfiles.about: Extensive despatch reviewing Soviet press coverage, Comintern resolutions, and theoretical analyses of the revolutionary movement in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reports on Moscow's heightened focus on Japan as a key frontline against anti-Soviet intervention following the invasion of Manchuria. Skinner provides detailed summaries and translations of theoretical writings, strike statistics, and speeches from Soviet publications, including Otto Kuusinen's report characterizing Japan as a predatory military-feudal imperialism vulnerable to agrarian revolt and monarchical collapse. An appended translation of the Twelfth ECCI Plenum theses outlines specific operational duties for the Japanese Communist Party to organize worker-peasant committees and oppose imperialist warfare.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 867: Russian Reports on Communism in Japan
